Count borrowers or count loans? Read an arrears rate’s denominator and threshold

Five charts separate published borrower 60+ and product-loan 90+ indicators from a fictional four-borrower tally. Learn how grouping accounts and changing thresholds alter a rate.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Count assigned status bands in a fixed sample of four fictional borrowers and eight accounts

Interactive planning lab

Fictional borrowers with at least one assigned 60+ account (out of 4)50.00%
Fictional assigned 90+ accounts (out of 8)25.00%
Fictional assigned 60+ accounts (out of 8)37.50%

The first two figures are fixed Bank of Canada published indicators based on TransUnion aggregates, updated 25 September 2026 and reviewed 25 October 2026. The borrower measure uses at least one 60+ account; product-loan measures use 90+. Downloadable FVI_FIN_STRESS metadata says households while the current public chart explicitly defines indebted borrowers; this guide follows the explicit chart definition and does not reconstruct households. Exact lender coverage, counts, joint-account handling and within-quarter timing are not supplied in the reviewed notes. The final three figures are a completely separate fictional counting sample: four borrowers A–D, exactly two outstanding toy accounts each, and each account belongs to only one borrower. C/D account codes remain 0; only A/B codes are editable. Codes are assigned teaching labels: 0 = below 60 days; 1 = 60–89 days; 2 = 90+ days. They are not calculated from dates, missed instalments, partial payments, agreements or credit reports. Code 0 does not mean never late. No actual borrower, reporting rule, legal status, lending decision, credit score or future-default probability is assessed. The toy’s fixed grouping is not a claim about TransUnion deduplication. Source rates stay unchanged when codes change.

The central idea

A rate needs both its counted unit and its qualifying condition. Several late accounts can belong to one borrower, and a 60-day borrower measure is different from a 90-day product-loan measure.

01

Read the counted unit and the qualifying condition together

The Bank of Canada’s credit-performance definitions distinguish two measures. The borrower indicator concerns indebted borrowers with at least one account whose payments are late by sixty days or more. Product indicators concern loans in a given class whose payments are late by ninety days or more.

Both can be expressed as percentages, but their numerators, denominators and thresholds differ. A borrower can have several accounts. An account can meet the sixty-day condition while remaining below ninety days. Treating every late account as another distinct borrower would change the unit being counted.

The first chart therefore presents the borrower indicator separately. The second presents six product-loan ratios, each using its own product-class denominator. The final three charts use a completely independent fictional sample to make the counting visible. None of the toy percentages estimates Canadian arrears.

02

Keep the quarter, publication vintage and adjustment attached to the rate

The source dashboard was updated on 25 September 2026 and reviewed here on 25 October 2026. The latest quarter in the reviewed official dataset is 2026 Q2. The borrower series shown begins in 2023 Q3 at 1.83% and ends at 2.23% in 2026 Q2.

The Bank’s notes identify TransUnion and Bank of Canada calculations, including X-13 seasonal adjustment of arrears rates. These are published adjusted indicators that can be revised. The labels identify reference quarters; they do not establish an exact day’s observation or an undocumented quarter-end count.

A rate meeting an arrears condition is also different from the number newly missing a payment during the quarter. Recoveries, exits, new qualifying accounts and changes in the denominator can affect a reported proportion. The point series alone cannot separate those flows or calculate an individual’s chance of becoming late next quarter.

03

Retain the source’s coverage and naming limitations

These are the Bank’s published Canadian indicators using TransUnion aggregates. The reviewed credit-performance notes do not establish an exact contributing-lender list, market-coverage fraction, original account counts, joint-account treatment or detailed population exclusions. A percentage does not reveal those missing denominators.

The source wording also needs care. Its current page includes household wording alongside an explicit indebted-borrower definition, and the downloaded financial-stress series description retains a household label. This guide follows the explicit borrower definition and current chart title. It does not construct households from account records or claim that one borrower represents an entire family.

The retrieved data provide point estimates without confidence intervals or quality grades. None is invented here. The product mortgage indicator is not a recovered CBA reporting-bank mortgage count, and the figures should not be extended to all lenders or all Canadians without the necessary coverage evidence.

04

Six product percentages are six different ratios

The latest product figures use the ninety-day-or-more condition. They describe loans within each named product class, rather than six mutually exclusive shares of the whole population.

2026 Q2 · product-loan 90+ rates · percent · seasonally adjusted
Product classPublished share
Mortgages0.23%
Automobile loans0.87%
Credit cards0.80%
Home equity lines of credit0.11%
Unsecured lines of credit0.40%
Instalment loans2.95%

Adding 0.23% for mortgages to 0.80% for credit cards would not produce a combined rate. A combined account rate would require the relevant loan counts and compatible definitions. An unweighted average would give each product class equal influence regardless of its size, which is not justified by these published percentages alone.

Likewise, the borrower rate of 2.23% cannot be divided by the mortgage rate of 0.23% to produce a meaningful personal-risk multiplier. One concerns any qualifying account per borrower at sixty days; the other concerns a particular loan class at ninety days. The differences do not isolate a causal effect of the product or rank a reader’s likelihood of default.

05

Build a small sample with explicit borrower–account grouping

The teaching sample has four fictional borrowers, A through D, with exactly two outstanding toy accounts each. Each account belongs to one borrower only. These assumptions make eight accounts and four distinct borrowers; they do not describe TransUnion’s handling of shared accounts or any real credit file.

Four controls assign labels to A1, A2, B1 and B2. Code 0 means below the sixty-day teaching threshold; code 1 means the sixty-to-eighty-nine band; code 2 means the ninety-or-more band. All four C/D accounts remain at code 0. The app accepts these category assignments directly rather than calculating status from dates, agreements, instalments or payment amounts.

At the defaults, A has codes 2 and 0, B has 1 and 2, and C and D have 0 and 0. The stacked bars group the two assigned accounts under each borrower. Every row totals two. Code 0 does not assert that an account has never been late; it only places it below the selected sixty-day threshold.

The fixed C/D assumptions also explain why the editable sample cannot make every borrower qualify. This is a bounded counting illustration, not a population simulator or an assessment of an actual repayment arrangement.

06

Count an already qualifying borrower only once

Borrowers A and B each have at least one code 1 or 2 account. The distinct-borrower numerator is therefore two, out of four borrowers: 50%. B has two qualifying accounts but remains one person in that numerator.

For the same sixty-day teaching condition, there are three qualifying accounts out of eight: A1, B1 and B2. The account share is 37.5%. This intermediate metric keeps the threshold fixed while changing the counted unit, showing the grouping effect separately.

The borrower ring displays four people in the selected fictional grouping; the account ring displays eight accounts. Their raw counts and denominators are available in the chart tables. The two rings are not two views of the same denominator, and their percentages should not be added.

If A1 is changed from code 2 to code 0 while the other defaults remain, A no longer has a qualifying account. The borrower count falls to one, even though B still has two qualifying accounts. That is a set-counting consequence of the assigned labels, not a prediction about real credit reporting.

07

Change the threshold effect without inventing a new borrower

At the defaults, the ninety-day teaching numerator contains only A1 and B2: two of eight accounts, or 25%. The sixty-day account numerator additionally includes B1, giving three of eight, or 37.5%. The denominator is the same eight accounts; the qualifying condition changes.

Now change only B1 from code 1 to code 2. The ninety-day account numerator rises from two to three, so its share becomes 37.5%. The sixty-day account numerator remains three, and the sixty-day borrower numerator remains A and B, giving 50%.

An additional account reaching the stricter assigned band does not necessarily add another borrower to the broader-band numerator. The displayed change is an alternative assignment in a fixed sample. It does not model the passage of time, a migration probability, a contractual delinquency rule or the effect of making a particular payment.

This is why a headline that says only “arrears rose” is incomplete. The reader needs the threshold, counted unit, population and reference period before interpreting what changed.

08

Use the public indicator as context and actual records for a payment plan

A published arrears indicator can describe a particular aggregate measure over time. It cannot supply the reader’s income, due dates, minimum payments, available cash or a lender’s treatment of an agreement. Those inputs belong in a separate dated household plan.

Keep credit utilization, payment obligations and arrears definitions distinct. A utilization ratio compares a reported balance with a limit; an arrears indicator applies a lateness condition. Neither can be substituted for the other merely because both concern credit accounts. The utilization guide examines that separate balance-and-snapshot question.

The controls on this page change fictional labels and their counts. They calculate no credit score, lending decision, legal status, collection process or future-default probability. The useful conclusion is narrower: the same accounts can generate different percentages when grouped by borrower or tested against a different assigned band, and the published rates must retain their own definitions.

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
